core_principles: The lunge is a multi-joint exercise that increases hip and knee extensor muscle strength.
The anterior limb generates significantly higher biceps femoris and gluteus maximus muscle activation compared to the posterior limb in both in-line and traditional lunges.
Vastus lateralis muscle activation does not significantly differ between in-line and traditional lunges, nor does it differ between the anterior and posterior leg positions.
The in-line lunge presents greater medio-lateral (ML) balance demands in the anterior limb compared to the traditional lunge.
specific_findings: Study population consisted of fifteen young, healthy, resistance-trained men (25 ± 5 years) performing exercises at their 10 repetition maximum.
Biceps femoris activity was significantly greater in the anterior compared to the posterior position for the in-line lunge (p = 0.003) and traditional lunge (p < 0.001).
Gluteus maximus activity was significantly greater in the anterior compared to posterior position for the in-line lunge (p < 0.001) and traditional lunge (p < 0.001).
Medio-lateral (ML) balance was significantly greater in the in-line exercise in the anterior limb (p = 0.001).

core_principles: In the traditional lunge, feet are positioned hip-width apart, whereas in the in-line lunge, feet are positioned at 50% hip-width apart.
Knee extensors and hip extensors act as the prime movers during lunges.
Hip abductors, such as the gluteus medius, act as secondary movers or stabilizers.
The in-line lunge provides a narrower base of support, creating a more challenging medio-lateral balance task.
Motor responses in the medio-lateral direction during narrow-base lunges are dominated by a hip strategy, stressing the hip adductors and abductors.
Proper execution in this protocol involves positioning the barbell in a high-bar alignment on the shoulders, with the forward knee flexed to 45 degrees before returning to full extension.
Maintain neutral alignment of the forward knee over the second metatarsal.
Keep the rear knee fully extended and both heels in contact with the floor throughout the movement.
common_mistakes: Allowing the forward knee to deviate from neutral alignment over the second metatarsal.
Losing heel contact with the floor during the movement.
Allowing the rear knee to flex during the stride-stance lunge.
specific_findings: In the traditional lunge, feet are hip-width apart, while in the in-line lunge, feet are positioned at 50% hip-width apart.

The study analyzed 15 young, healthy, resistance-trained men (age: 25 ± 5 years, height: 175.7 ± 7.7 cm, mass: 81 ± 8 kg, 10RM of traditional lunge: 52.9 ± 14.4 kg, with 5 ± 2 years of training experience).
A pilot study of n = 5 was used to determine that 14 subjects were needed for an alpha level of 0.05 and statistical power of 0.80.
The protocol required the forward knee to be flexed to 45 degrees.
Motor responses in the medio-lateral direction were dominated by a hip strategy, citing Jancová (2008).

core_principles: Perform lunge variations (traditional and in-line) with a controlled cadence, such as 60 beats per minute.
Maintain a continuous movement without stopping between the eccentric (lowering) and concentric (rising) phases of the lunge.
Allow adequate rest (at least 5 minutes between heavy load adjustments and 30 minutes between different lunge variations) to prevent neuromuscular fatigue.
Refrain from strenuous lower body exercise for at least 48 hours prior to maximal strength testing to ensure accurate performance and recovery.
common_mistakes: Pausing or stopping between the eccentric and concentric phases of the lunge.
Insufficient rest between maximal effort sets, leading to premature neuromuscular fatigue.
specific_findings: The study compared four experimental lunge conditions: (1) traditional lunge with dominant leg in front, (2) traditional lunge with dominant leg in back, (3) in-line lunge with dominant leg in front, and (4) in-line lunge with dominant leg in back.
Subjects performed a 10-repetition maximum (10RM) test at a 60 beat cadence.
Load adjustments for the 10RM test were made by 4–10 kg when the target reps were not achieved on the first attempt.
sEMG signals were recorded at a sampling rate of 2000 Hz.
VL electrode placement was at 2/3 of the distance between the anterior spina iliac and the superior aspect of the lateral side of the patella.
BF electrode placement was at 50% on the line between the ischial tuberosity and the lateral epicondyle of the tibia.
GM electrode placement was at 50% of the distance between the sacral vertebrae and the greater trochanter.
GMd electrode placement was at 50% on the line from the iliac crest to the trochanter.
For VL and BF MVICs, subjects were seated with their knee flexed at 90º and the strap placed on the distal tibia.
For GM MVIC, subjects laid prone with their knee flexed at 90º and the strap placed on the distal region of the thigh.
For GMd MVIC, subjects laid prone with their knee extended and the strap placed on the distal region of both lower limbs in hip abduction.
Mediolateral (ML) displacement of the center of pressure was assessed using a Wii Fit Balance Board under the anterior lower limb with a sampling rate of 37 Hz, calibrated with a weight of 10 kgf.

core_principles: Traditional and in-line lunges elicit similar overall muscle activation in the lower limbs.
Biceps femoris and gluteus maximus activity is significantly higher in the anterior (front) leg compared to the posterior (back) leg during both lunge variations.
Vastus lateralis and gluteus medius activation levels do not significantly differ between the front and back legs.
The in-line lunge demands significantly greater mediolateral balance control compared to the traditional lunge.
Stance width variations between traditional and in-line lunges do not alter sagittal plane muscle activation of the prime movers or stabilizers.
specific_findings: Biceps Femoris activity was significantly greater in the anterior compared to the posterior position: in-line (p = 0.003; d = 1.19; Δ% = 53) and traditional (p < 0.001; d = 1.69; Δ% = 68.3).
Gluteus Maximus activity was significantly greater in the anterior compared to the posterior position: in-line (p < 0.001; d = 3.96; Δ% = 87.7) and traditional (p < 0.001; d = 3.45; Δ% = 88.3).

Mediolateral balance displacement was significantly greater in the in-line exercise in the anterior limb (19.4 ± 4.1 cm) compared to the traditional lunge (14.8 ± 2.9 cm; p = 0.001; d = 0.81; Δ% = 23.51).
Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICCs) for all RMS data ranged between 0.91 and 0.98.

core_principles: The lunge is a complex multi-joint task requiring coordination of monoarticular and biarticular muscles across the knee and hip.
The anterior and posterior legs experience highly distinct mechanical demands and muscle activation profiles, meaning each leg must be analyzed separately.
The anterior leg functions similarly to a squat, with the vastus lateralis (VL) acting as a primary knee stabilizer and prime mover.
The posterior leg exhibits significantly lower biceps femoris (BF) and gluteus maximus (GM) activation compared to the anterior leg.
Vastus lateralis (VL) activation remains similar between both the anterior and posterior legs due to comparable knee range of motion (0 to 90 degrees).
Narrowing the stance width (as in an in-line lunge) reduces the base of support, significantly challenging mediolateral (ML) balance and requiring a hip-dominant stabilization strategy.
Muscles of the anterior limb during a lunge may experience a 'sticking region' where muscle fiber length and myofilament overlap are suboptimal for maximal force production.
common_mistakes: Failing to stabilize the hip and core to counter the increased mediolateral instability caused by a narrower stance width (in-line lunge).
specific_findings: The highest muscle activation was observed in the VL (Δ% = ~53.4, for both exercises).
The GM presented lower muscle activity when compared to the BF (Δ% = ~6, for both exercises).
The ROM of the knee joint was similar in both leg positions (0-90 degrees).
The in-line lunge showed greater ML balance when compared to the traditional exercise (Δ% = 23.51).

core_principles: Both traditional and in-line lunges demonstrate similar overall levels of lower limb muscle activation.
The anterior limb in a lunge generates higher activation of the biceps femoris and gluteus maximus compared to the posterior limb.
The vastus lateralis shows similar activation levels between both the front and back legs, as well as between traditional and in-line lunge variations.
The gluteus medius acts primarily in the frontal plane of the hip joint to stabilize the pelvis during the sagittal plane movement of the lunge.
The in-line lunge is highly recommended for challenging and training medio-lateral balance and stability under load.
specific_findings: The anterior limb generated the highest biceps femoris (BF) and gluteus maximus (GM) muscle activation when compared to the posterior limb.
The vastus lateralis (VL) showed similar activation between legs and exercises.
The in-line lunge showed greater medio-lateral (ML) balance demands when compared to the traditional lunge.
The study utilized a Wii Fit Balance Board to analyze medio-lateral (ML) balance.

core_principles: In-line and traditional lunge variations differ in their demands on balance and lower limb muscle activation.
Knee joint-angle positions during squatting exercises significantly affect muscle activation levels.
Joint position influences electromyographic (EMG) activity and torque generation of the hamstrings and gluteus maximus during isometric contractions.
